PullRequest.Title: Add MCP customization migration
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

- Add an MCP server migration category to the Agent Customizations editor, behind `chat.customizations.mcpServerMigration.enabled`.
- Move eligible workspace server entries from `.vscode/mcp.json` to workspace-root `.mcp.json` so the active Agent Host harness can discover them directly.
- Show source and destination before confirmation, preserve selection and keyboard focus across refreshes, and leave unsupported or unselected servers in place.

<details>
<summary>Technical context for AI-assisted review</summary>

### Eligibility and editor integration

The migration service extends its existing support reporting with executable MCP candidates. Candidates must be enabled, applicable to the session, client-forwarded, fully supported, and exactly representable in the destination format. The source configuration must match the current Agent Host delivery projection without losing properties or relying on unresolved configuration variables.

MCP entries reuse the editor's existing virtualized migration lists, grouping, selection, confirmation, and notification flow. They are server entries rather than customization files, so rows show a name and source-to-destination path without file-specific actions. Existing prompt, user-data, and configured-location migration behavior is preserved.

### Session context and URI routing

The service recomputes eligibility after confirmation and checks the active session and ordered working-directory roots before and between writes. The support scope remains live during execution. Guards compare coverage and the pending candidates' delivery eligibility and projected configuration, rather than support-snapshot object identity, so equivalent snapshot refreshes do not abort migration merely because a new object was published.

`IAgentHostCustomizationService.getWorkingDirectoryUris` derives client-resolvable roots in the shared abstract service. Existing root getters retain host-side URI strings for workspace classification and protocol enablement decisions. The Agents Window uses the provider's stable resource mapper instead of depending on a feedback channel or falling back to identity mapping, preventing remote roots from being mistaken for matching local paths.

Workbench root resolution uses provisional roots until session state is available and falls back to the subscription's verified state on errors. MCP computation honors caller cancellation while waiting for initial support resolution, checks cancellation around planning, and disposes the acquired support scope.

### Write safety and failure handling

Each source/destination pair is handled as a guarded two-file update:

1. Re-read the source and destination, reject changed source entries and conflicting destination entries.
2. Write missing destination entries first, or accept equivalent entries already present.
3. Recheck execution context before removing the selected source entries.
4. Re-read both files to verify the result; restore original content only when doing so is safe.

Existing wrapped (`mcpServers`) and flat JSONC `.mcp.json` files are accepted. Edits preserve surrounding comments and formatting. Existing-file writes compare exact expected content and use file-service etag/mtime guards; new-file creation does not overwrite an existing destination.

These are best-effort optimistic-concurrency checks, not an atomic cross-file transaction. If rollback cannot be performed safely, the operation reports a structured failure and asks the user to review the affected files. A newly created destination is retained rather than deleted during rollback. Planning exclusions and execution phases are trace-logged for diagnosis.

</details>

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The nested sequential loops and all three call sites are explicit, tests exercise multiple roots, and the caller passes the complete ordered session root list. Exact wall-clock cost varies by filesystem/provider, but the quadratic call count and critical-path placement are deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: filesystem read operations against `.mcp.json` and `.vscode/mcp.json`, including remote file-provider calls
Findings.PerformanceScaling: With G selected source/target groups and R workspace roots, this call runs once per group and reads two files for every other root; `migrateGroup` repeats the same scan twice more, so the successful path performs about 6*G*(R-1) cross-root reads in addition to each group's own reads. When one group is selected per root, this is quadratic in the root count.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: excessive filesystem I/O and migration latency, especially for remote multi-root workspaces where the reads are sequential IPC/network round trips
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no MCP customization migration execution path, so confirming a migration performed none of these cross-root filesystem scans.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new execution loop invokes `findCrossRootConflicts` for every migration group; that helper serially reads both MCP configuration locations in every other workspace root, and the same full-root scan is invoked again after the target write and after verification.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added line 224 places a complete all-roots filesystem scan inside the newly added per-group loop; added calls in `migrateGroup` repeat that scan at two later phases.
Findings.Title: Avoid rescanning every root for each migration group
Findings.Impact: Confirming migration for servers spread across a 10-root workspace causes roughly 540 cross-root conflict reads before counting source/target verification and write guards, and the nested loops await them serially. On remote filesystems this can turn a one-click migration into a long-running operation.
Findings.Evidence: `executeMigration` processes `groups.values()` sequentially and line 224 awaits `findCrossRootConflicts(group, workingDirectories, fileService)`. `findCrossRootConflicts` loops every root and awaits `readTargetDocument` plus `readSourceDocument`; `migrateGroup` then calls `ensureNoCrossRootConflicts` after writing the target and once more after `verifyMigration`, each of which calls the same scanner. The service supplies all session roots through `migrate(..., { roots })`, so G can equal R in a normal multi-root migration.
Findings.Recommendation: Build a conflict index by reading each root's source and target once per validation phase, then check all groups against that index. Preserve concurrency safety by refreshing only roots whose files may have changed after each write (or track etag/mtime and re-read changed documents), rather than rescanning every file for every group.

Scenarios.Scenario: Migration availability badges and the open Customizations editor recompute eligible MCP candidates after session, inventory, definition, enablement, or workbench changes.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The badge/editor cannot publish its new candidate count/list until the MCP support scope resolves and candidate planning reads and parses each eligible workspace source file. Rendering the loading state is synchronous; support assessment and filesystem planning are awaited.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read and parse `.vscode/mcp.json` for each workspace root represented by an otherwise-deliverable server.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One read per distinct eligible source URI within a single plan; effective cardinality is at most the number of session roots. The per-plan ResourceMap deduplicates servers from the same source, but there is no cache across refresh calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: MCP support reporting did not inspect workspace configuration files to produce executable candidates; file migration categories retained their existing reads.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Candidate count and editor migration data wait for all source reads.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct session workspace roots containing deliverable MCP server definitions, after same-source deduplication, plus the frequency of MCP refresh signals.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Migration categories run with Promise.all. Within MCP planning, a new source read is awaited when first encountered, effectively serializing distinct roots. The support scope debounces its own assessment by 50 ms; the availability service coalesces same-tick signals with RunOnceScheduler, while editor refreshes can overlap and discard stale results without canceling their work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The ref-counted support scope is reused only while overlapping callers hold it and debounces support recomputation. Source-file reads are cached only inside one createPlan call; warm refreshes reread files, and missing files are not negatively cached across calls.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed listeners, await paths, per-plan deduplication, support-scope debounce, and source reads are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: MCP migration is experimental/default-off and typical root counts are small. Signal frequency and remote provider latency vary, so repeated editor/availability planning did not independently meet the reporting threshold.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding. Refresh work is gated for the global availability service and per-plan source reads are grouped; editor refresh lacks equivalent coalescing, but realistic sustained frequency and impact were not established strongly enough for an additional performance finding.

Scenarios.Scenario: User confirms migration of selected MCP servers from `.vscode/mcp.json` to root `.mcp.json` across a multi-root workspace.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The confirmation remains in progress until re-planning, all guarded group writes, conflict scans, verification, and any rollback complete. Every conflict scan and file guard is awaited on the execution path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recompute the current plan by reading each eligible source file before execution.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One source read per distinct eligible source root before selected candidates are matched.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No MCP migration execution or re-planning existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Migration does not begin writing until the fresh plan completes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read source and target documents, scan other roots for duplicate names, perform guarded target/source writes, verify both documents, and conditionally restore them.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: For G selected source groups and R roots, cross-root conflict checks perform about 6*G*(R-1) reads on a successful write path because each group scans every other root before migration, after the target write, and after verification; own-document reads/resolves/writes add O(G). With G=R this is quadratic.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Before the PR this workflow and all associated filesystem operations were absent.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All groups and each root within a conflict scan are awaited sequentially, so remote provider round-trip latency accumulates before completion.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of distinct selected source/target root groups and total ordered session roots; server names are grouped per source pair, so effective group cardinality, not raw server count, controls the cross-root fan-out.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Groups are processed sequentially. Each conflict scan loops roots sequentially and reads target then source sequentially. There is no limiter because there is no parallelism; ordering provides safety but also sums every boundary latency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Planning deduplicates source reads only within that plan. Execution does not cache cross-root source/target documents across groups or across its three validation phases. Existing-file write guards deliberately reread current content/metadata; missing target/source reads are repeated rather than negatively cached.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: nested loops, three full conflict-scan call sites, grouping behavior, sequential awaits, and caller-provided complete root list are explicit and covered by multi-root tests.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Most workspaces have few roots, but multi-root workspaces with roughly 10 or more roots are realistic, and remote file-provider latency varies. This affects severity, not the deterministic quadratic mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported a medium-severity boundary-fanout regression because the new workflow performs deterministic quadratic, sequential filesystem I/O on its user-visible completion path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent Host session/root hydration and mapping between host URI space and client filesystem URI space.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Root getters synchronously resolve the in-memory session target/subscription state and map each root URI; no file, IPC, subprocess, database, or network operation is introduced on the getter path itself.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of ordered working-directory roots in the active session.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous in-memory mapping; subscription updates trigger existing customization events.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Session subscriptions are retained/reused by backend session and connection. Mapping allocates a new URI array per getter call but does not retain it or introduce an unbounded cache.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: getter and subscription code were inspected directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Root arrays are normally small; call frequency increases during migration context checks but URI parsing/mapping remains minor relative to filesystem work.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression; mapping is linear in root count and enables correct client-side file access without a new expensive boundary.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass across all 24 changed files. Traced migration discovery, editor refresh, support-scope lifecycle, root mapping, and guarded execution. Submitted one finding for quadratic sequential cross-root filesystem fan-out during multi-root MCP migration; no regression-fix learning signal was applicable.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
